title: Animals with a backbone: five groups and how to tell them apart

summary.text: A fish, a frog, a lizard, a crow and you all have a backbone, a chain of small bones down the middle of the back. Animals with a backbone are called vertebrates. Scientists sort them into five groups: fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals. You tell the groups apart by checking more than one clue. The clues are what covers the body, how they breathe, and how their babies start life. Your child feels their own backbone, then makes a straw backbone to find out how a chain of hard bones can bend.
summary.art: A row of five animals side by side, a sardine, a frog, a house gecko, a crow and a girl, each with a dotted line showing the chain of small bones along their back.

intro.hook: Ask a grown-up to bend forward. Run your fingers down the middle of their back. You feel a row of hard bumps. Is that one long bone, or many?
intro.text: The bumps you feel are bones. Together they make the backbone. A fish has a backbone too, and so do a frog, a lizard, a crow and a cow. An ant, a prawn and an earthworm do not have one. In this unit you meet the five groups of animals with a backbone. You learn the clues that tell them apart. And you build a backbone from a straw, to find out how a row of hard bones can bend.
intro.art: A child running her fingers down the back of a grown-up who bends forward, with a row of small bumps showing along the spine.

outcomes: By the end I can find my own backbone and say that it is a chain of many small bones called vertebrae.
By the end I can say that animals with a backbone are vertebrates, and animals without one, like ants and prawns, are invertebrates.
By the end I can name the five groups of vertebrates, fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals, and give an animal from each.
By the end I can tell the groups apart with clues: what covers the body, how they breathe, how the babies start, and whether mothers make milk.
By the end I can sort a tricky animal, like a bat, a turtle or a pangolin, by checking more than one clue.
By the end I can make a guess with a reason, test a straw backbone fairly, count what I see and say what I found.
By the end I can say that humans are mammals, and that we are animals with a backbone like the rest.

terms.meaning: The backbone is the row of small bones down the middle of your back, from your neck to your bottom. Its other name is the spine.
terms.example: When you bend forward, you can feel the bumps of your backbone under the skin.
terms.art: A child seen from behind, bending forward, with the bumps of the backbone showing in a line.

terms.meaning: A vertebra is one of the small bones that make up the backbone. Many of them together are called vertebrae (say VER-tuh-bray).
terms.example: You have 33 vertebrae. A snake has a few hundred.
terms.art: Three small round bones stacked in a short row, each with a ring-shaped hole in the middle.

terms.meaning: A vertebrate is an animal with a backbone.
terms.example: A crow, a frog, a goldfish and you are all vertebrates.
terms.art: A crow, a frog, a goldfish and a boy standing in a row.

terms.meaning: An invertebrate is an animal with no backbone.
terms.example: Ants, prawns, earthworms, snails and spiders are invertebrates.
terms.art: An ant, a prawn, an earthworm and a snail on a leaf.

terms.meaning: Fish are vertebrates that live in water, breathe with gills and swim with fins. Most have scales.
terms.example: A sardine (mathi), a rohu and a seahorse are fish.
terms.art: A silver sardine and a rohu swimming, with fins and scales showing.

terms.meaning: Gills are the parts behind a fish's head that take in oxygen from the water. Oxygen is a gas in air and water that every animal needs.
terms.example: Lift the flap behind a fish's eye, and the red gills are underneath.
terms.art: The side of a fish's head with the flap lifted, showing red, comb-like gills.

terms.meaning: An amphibian is a vertebrate with smooth, damp skin and no scales. Most start life in water as tadpoles and later live on land too.
terms.example: Frogs and toads are amphibians. The word means 'two lives', in water and on land.
terms.art: A green frog sitting at the edge of a pond, half in the water.

terms.meaning: A tadpole is a baby frog or toad. A tadpole lives in water, has a tail, and breathes with gills.
terms.example: In the monsoon, puddles and ponds can fill with black tadpoles.
terms.art: Small black tadpoles with round bodies and wriggly tails in shallow water.

terms.meaning: A reptile is a vertebrate with dry skin covered in scales. Reptiles breathe with lungs, and most lay eggs on land.
terms.example: The house gecko, the cobra, the turtle and the crocodile are reptiles.
terms.art: A house gecko on a wall, a turtle and a crocodile resting on a riverbank.

terms.meaning: Scales are small, hard plates that cover the skin of fish and reptiles.
terms.example: You can see the shiny scales on a fish at the market, and dry scales on a snake's skin.
terms.art: Close-up of overlapping scales on a fish next to the dry scales of a snake.

terms.meaning: A bird is a vertebrate with feathers, a beak, two legs and two wings. Every bird hatches from an egg with a hard shell.
terms.example: Crows, sparrows, hens and peacocks are birds.
terms.art: A crow, a sparrow, a hen and a peacock standing together.

terms.meaning: A mammal is a vertebrate with hair or fur, whose mother feeds the babies milk.
terms.example: Cows, dogs, bats, elephants and humans are mammals.
terms.art: A cow feeding her calf, a dog and a bat hanging upside down.

explanations.concept: A backbone is a chain of small bones
explanations.context: This card is about what a backbone is made of, and what it does.
explanations.definition: A backbone is a row of small bones, called vertebrae, joined one after another along the back.
explanations.description: Your backbone is not one long bone. It is a chain of 33 small bones called vertebrae, with soft pads between them. Each joint tilts only a little, but many small tilts add up, so your back can bend a lot. Every vertebra has a hole in the middle, and the spinal cord runs through the holes. The spinal cord is a thick bundle of nerves that carries messages between your brain and your body. So the backbone holds you up, lets you bend, and keeps your spinal cord safe.
examples: You have 33 vertebrae.
A snake has a few hundred, so a snake can curl up into rings.
A frog has only about nine, so a frog's back is short and stiff.
A giraffe and you both have 7 bones in the neck. The giraffe's neck bones are just much longer.
explanations.art: A side view of a person's backbone, a curving chain of small bones from the skull to the hips, with soft pads between them.

explanations.context: This card is about the two kinds of animals: with a backbone, and without.
explanations.definition: Vertebrates are animals with a backbone. Invertebrates are animals without one.
explanations.description: A crow, a goat, a frog and a fish all have a backbone, so they are vertebrates. An ant, a prawn, a spider and an earthworm have no backbone, so they are invertebrates. A prawn has a hard covering, but it is on the outside of the body, not a row of bones inside. Most kinds of animals in the world are invertebrates. Only about 1 in every 20 known kinds of animal has a backbone.
examples: Vertebrates: a crow, a cat, a frog, a cobra, a sardine, you.
Invertebrates: an ant, a prawn, a crab, a snail, an earthworm, a butterfly.
explanations.art: A crow and a cat on one side with their backbones drawn as dotted lines, and an ant and a prawn on the other side with no backbone.

explanations.context: This card is about the first of the five groups: fish.
explanations.definition: Fish live in water, breathe with gills and swim with fins. Most fish are covered in scales.
explanations.description: A fish takes water in through the mouth and pushes it out over the gills. The gills take oxygen from the water. Fins help a fish steer and stay upright, and the tail pushes the fish along. Most fish lay many tiny eggs in the water. About half of all the kinds of vertebrates in the world are fish.
examples: A sardine (mathi) from the sea off Kerala.
A rohu from a pond in Bengal.
A seahorse, who swims upright.
A shark, who is a fish too.
explanations.art: A silver sardine with labels pointing to the gill flap, the fins, the scales and the tail.

explanations.context: This card is about the second group: amphibians, such as frogs and toads.
explanations.definition: Amphibians have smooth, damp skin with no scales. Most begin life in water as tadpoles, then live on land and in water.
explanations.description: A frog lays soft eggs in jelly, in water. A tadpole hatches, with a tail and gills, like a small fish. Slowly the tadpole grows legs, loses the tail and becomes a frog. A grown frog breathes with lungs, and also through the damp skin. That is why frogs stay in damp places. Amphibians include frogs, toads, and caecilians, who have no legs and live in wet soil in the Western Ghats and the Northeast.
examples: The common Indian toad, seen on wet roads in the monsoon.
A tree frog with sticky toe pads.
The purple frog of the Western Ghats, who lives underground most of the year. The Indian scientist S. D. Biju described her in 2003.
A caecilian, who looks like a big earthworm but has a backbone.
explanations.art: A row: frog eggs in jelly, a tadpole, a tadpole with back legs, a young frog with a short tail, and a grown frog.

explanations.context: This card is about the third group: reptiles, such as lizards, snakes, turtles and crocodiles.
explanations.definition: Reptiles have dry skin covered in scales. They breathe with lungs, and most lay eggs on land.
explanations.description: A reptile's scales are dry, not slimy. A snake's skin feels dry and smooth, like a leather bag. Reptiles breathe air with lungs, even turtles and crocodiles who spend a lot of time in water. Most reptiles lay eggs with a tough shell, in sand, soil or a nest of leaves. A few snakes, like the Russell's viper, give birth to babies instead.
examples: The house gecko near the tube light.
The spectacled cobra.
The olive ridley sea turtles who lay eggs on Odisha's beaches.
The mugger crocodile in rivers and lakes.
explanations.art: A mother olive ridley turtle digging a nest in the sand of a beach at night.

explanations.context: This card is about the fourth group: birds.
explanations.definition: Birds have feathers, a beak, two legs and two wings. Every bird hatches from an egg with a hard shell.
explanations.description: Feathers are the clue that only birds have. A bird breathes with lungs, and has no teeth, only a beak. Every bird lays eggs with a hard shell, and the parents usually keep the eggs warm. Most birds can fly, but not all. A hen can only flutter up a little way, and an ostrich cannot fly at all.
examples: A crow on the window ledge.
A sparrow in a hole in a wall.
A hen with her eggs.
A peacock, India's national bird.
explanations.art: A crow on a window ledge with labels on the feathers, beak, wing and two legs.

explanations.context: This card is about the fifth group: mammals. Humans are in this group.
explanations.definition: Mammals have hair or fur, and the mothers feed their babies milk.
explanations.description: Mammals breathe with lungs. Most mammals give birth to babies, not eggs. Every mammal mother makes milk for her young. Mammals come in many shapes: a bat flies, a river dolphin swims, and an elephant walks. Humans are mammals too. You have hair, you breathe with lungs, and you drank milk as a baby. So you are an animal with a backbone, one mammal among many.
examples: A cow and her calf.
An Indian flying fox, a big bat, hanging in a tree.
The Ganga river dolphin, India's national aquatic animal.
You.
explanations.art: A mother goat feeding her kid, next to a mother holding her baby.

explanations.concept: Tricky animals: check more than one clue
explanations.context: This card is about animals who look as if they belong to one group, but really belong to another.
explanations.definition: To sort an animal into a group, check several clues, not just one: the covering, the breathing, the babies and milk.
explanations.description: Some animals fool us if we look at only one clue. A bat flies, but has fur, and the mother feeds her baby milk, so a bat is a mammal. A river dolphin swims with fins, but breathes air and drinks milk as a baby, so she is a mammal. A turtle swims in the sea, but has dry scales and lungs, so she is a reptile. A pangolin is covered in scales, but has some hair and feeds her baby milk, so she is a mammal. A caecilian has no legs, like a snake, but has smooth damp skin, so they are an amphibian.
examples: Bat: flies, but a mammal.
River dolphin: swims, but a mammal.
Pangolin: scales, but a mammal.
Turtle: swims in the sea, but a reptile.
Flying lizard of the Western Ghats: glides on skin flaps, but a reptile.
explanations.art: An Indian pangolin walking, with big brown scales, and a baby pangolin riding on her tail.

explanations.context: This card is about a question scientists argue about: whether five groups is the best way to sort vertebrates.
explanations.description: Most school books use five groups, and the five are easy to tell apart. But some scientists sort animals by their family tree: who is whose closest relative. Seen that way, the groups look different.
examples: Sharks and sardines are both called fish, but they are only distant cousins.
A crocodile's closest living relatives are birds, not lizards.

perspectives.explanation: Five groups are useful. Each one has clues you can see, like feathers or damp skin. So anyone can sort a new animal quickly.

perspectives.who: Scientists who draw family trees of animals
perspectives.explanation: Groups should hold relatives. Birds and crocodiles came from the same ancestors, so birds belong inside the reptile family. And 'fish' is really several groups.

explanations.art: A simple family tree with branches ending in a shark, a sardine, a frog, a lizard, a crocodile, a bird and a cow.

agreed.text: Animals with a backbone are vertebrates, and every vertebrate has a backbone made of many small vertebrae.
agreed.evidence: Scientists have looked at the skeletons of thousands of kinds of fish, frogs, reptiles, birds and mammals. Every one has a backbone made of separate vertebrae.

agreed.text: Vertebrates can be sorted into fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals, by clues such as covering, breathing, eggs and milk.
agreed.evidence: These clues hold for almost every animal. All birds have feathers, and all mammal mothers make milk. Scientists still argue about how the groups fit on the family tree.

agreed.text: Humans are mammals, so humans are animals too.
agreed.evidence: Humans have hair, breathe with lungs, have a backbone of vertebrae, and are fed milk as babies, just like other mammals.

agreed.text: All vertebrates come from the same ancestors, small animals like fish who lived in the sea more than 500 million years ago.
agreed.evidence: The oldest fossils of animals with a backbone are more than 500 million years old, and all are from the sea. The genes of all vertebrates show they are related.

challenging.claim: A river dolphin is a fish, because she lives in water and has fins.
challenging.for: Dolphins live in water all their lives, swim with fins and a tail, and have a smooth body like many fish.
challenging.against: A dolphin breathes air through a hole on the top of her head, and has no gills. Her baby drinks her milk. So she is a mammal.
challenging.context: This card is about sorting an animal by where they live.

challenging.for: Snakes look shiny, and many people think shiny means wet.
challenging.against: Snake skin is dry. The shine comes from smooth scales. Frogs and toads are the ones with damp skin.
challenging.context: This card is about how reptile skin feels.

challenging.who: An old idea, still held by some scientists
challenging.for: Fish brains are built differently from ours. Fish do not cry out or make faces when hurt.
challenging.against: Fish feel pain and fear. In 2003 the British scientist Lynne Sneddon found nerves on the faces of trout that sense harm. Trout given a sting rocked from side to side, rubbed their lips on the gravel, and were slow to start eating again. Some scientists still argue that fish only react, without the feeling.
challenging.context: This card is about whether fish feel pain.

challenging.claim: Birds should be counted as reptiles.
challenging.who: Many scientists who study family trees
challenging.for: Birds come from dinosaurs, who were reptiles. A bird's closest living relative is the crocodile. Birds have scales on their legs and lay eggs with shells, like reptiles.
challenging.against: Birds have feathers, and they make their own body heat, which most reptiles do not. Many scientists find it more useful to keep birds as a group of their own.
challenging.context: This card is about where birds belong.

big_questions.q: Your backbone is many small bones working together. Are you one thing, or many things working together?
big_questions.hint: Think of the straw backbone. Was it one thing or eight pieces? Can it be both?

big_questions.q: A pangolin has scales like a lizard, but is a mammal. Who decides which group an animal is in: nature, or people?
big_questions.hint: Did the pangolin know she was a mammal? Who made up the word 'mammal'?

big_questions.q: A fish, a frog and you all have a backbone. What else might you share with a fish?
big_questions.hint: Think about eyes, a mouth, a heart and blood.

big_questions.q: Why might so few kinds of animals have a backbone, when so many have none?
big_questions.hint: Think of ants and beetles. They are small and there are so many of them. Does a small animal need a backbone?

big_questions.q: What does a frog feel when the first monsoon rain falls?
big_questions.hint: Frogs come out and call loudly when the rain comes. Why might that be?

story.title: The Chain in the Fish
story.note: A made-up story. A cooked fish's backbone really does lift out as a chain of small bones. Prawns have no backbone. Bats are mammals: they have fur and feed their babies milk.
text: Meenakshi was seven. She lived in a flat in Mangaluru with Amma, her grandmother Ajji and her little brother Kiran, who was five.
One Sunday, Ajji fried bangude for lunch. Bangude is the Tulu and Kannada name for mackerel, a fish from the sea. There was also a bowl of prawns in red masala.

'Watch,' said Ajji. She pressed her fingers along the top of the fish. Then she held the tail and lifted. A long white bone came out in one piece, with thin side bones sticking out like the teeth of a comb.

Meenakshi put the bone on her plate. She looked closely. It was not one long stick. It was a row of tiny bones, joined end to end, like beads on a thread. She tried to count them, but there were so many that she lost count.
She held the bone at both ends and bent it very gently. The row curved like a bow.
'That chain is the fish's backbone,' said Ajji. 'Each little bone in it is called a vertebra. Many of them are called vertebrae.'
'Ver-te-bray,' said Kiran, and laughed at the word.
Then Kiran picked up a prawn. He pulled off the hard pink shell. Inside was soft white meat. 'Where is the prawn's backbone?' he asked.
Meenakshi looked. There were no bones at all. 'The prawn has no backbone,' she said. 'The hard part is the shell, on the outside.'
'Yes,' said Ajji. 'Animals with a backbone are called vertebrates. Animals without one, like prawns and ants, are invertebrates.'
'Do I have a backbone?' asked Kiran.
'Bend over and touch your toes,' said Meenakshi. Kiran bent over. Meenakshi ran her finger down the middle of his back. Under his vest she felt a row of hard bumps, from his neck down to his shorts.
'Kiran is a chain too!' she said.
Kiran stood up and wriggled. 'I am a bendy chain,' he said. 'Like the fish.'

After lunch, Meenakshi sat at the window with her notebook. She wrote two lists: 'Backbone' and 'No backbone'. A crow landed on the ledge. 'A crow has a backbone,' said Ajji. 'So does the gecko behind the tube light.' The ants on the ledge went in the other list.
'So all the backbone animals are one big family?' asked Meenakshi.

'They are all related,' said Ajji. 'Scientists sort them into five groups.' She held up one hand and spread her fingers. 'Fish. Amphibians, like frogs. Reptiles, like lizards and snakes. Birds. And mammals.'
'How do you know which group an animal is in?' asked Meenakshi.

'You look for clues,' said Ajji. She touched each finger. 'Fish have fins and gills. Amphibians have smooth, wet skin. Reptiles have dry scales. Birds have feathers. Mammals have hair, and their mothers feed them milk.'
That evening the sky turned orange. Big bats flew over the coconut trees, flapping slowly.
'Birds!' said Kiran.
Meenakshi thought about the clues. 'Bats fly, like birds,' she said. 'But do they have feathers?'
'No,' said Ajji. 'A bat's body is covered in fur. And a bat mother feeds her baby milk.'
'Fur and milk,' said Meenakshi. 'Then a bat is a mammal, not a bird.'
'Flying is only one clue,' said Ajji. 'Always check more than one.'
Kiran was quiet for a moment. Then he asked, 'What group am I in?'
Meenakshi counted on her fingers. 'You have a backbone. You have hair. You breathe air. And Amma fed you milk when you were a baby.' She smiled. 'You are a mammal.'
'So I am an animal?' asked Kiran.
'Yes,' said Ajji. 'Humans are mammals, and mammals are animals. So are you, and so am I.'

That night Meenakshi drew two pictures side by side. One was the fish's backbone, a long row of tiny bones. The other was Kiran bending over, with a row of bumps down his back. Under them she wrote: 'Fish, frog, lizard, crow, bat, Kiran and me. We each have a chain of bones.'
story.epiphany: For the parent: Meenakshi sees that a backbone is a chain of small bones, in a fish and in her brother. She learns the five groups, and finds out with the bats that one clue, like flying, can fool you. Kiran finds out that humans are mammals, and so animals too.
ask: What did Meenakshi see when she looked closely at the fish's backbone?
Why did the prawn have no backbone to find?
Kiran thought the bats were birds. Which two clues showed they are mammals?

Close-up of a fish backbone on a steel plate: a row of tiny bones joined end to end, with thin side bones.
A girl running her finger down her little brother's back while he bends over to touch his toes.

experiments.title: Bendy Backbone: how many pieces does a backbone need to bend?
experiments.context: In this experiment you make a pretend backbone from a straw threaded on wool. First the straw is in one piece. Then you cut it into 2, 4 and 8 pieces. Each time you wrap it round a steel tumbler and see how well it bends.
experiments.question: Does a backbone bend better when it is one long piece, or many short pieces?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Which will wrap round the tumbler best: 1 long piece, 2 pieces, 4 pieces or 8 short pieces? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: We use the same straw every time, so the total length stays the same. We use the same wool, the same tumbler and the same gentle pull. Only the number of pieces changes. That way, any difference comes from the number of pieces.
results_table: How many pieces touch the tumbler
Biggest gap: how many fingers fit?

materials.item: a paper or plastic drinking straw, or a tube of newspaper rolled tightly round a pencil and taped
a piece of wool or thick thread, about as long as your arm
a little sticky tape, to make a stiff tip on the wool
a steel tumbler
children's scissors
a pencil and paper for the results

schedule.what: Test a straw backbone in 1, 2, 4 and 8 pieces round a tumbler. Count, draw and compare.

experiments.record: Fill in the results table. Draw the shape each chain made round the tumbler.

setup.art: A paper drinking straw threaded on a long piece of wool, next to a steel tumbler and a pair of children's scissors.
setup.caption: 1. Thread one whole straw onto the wool.

setup.art: Hands wrapping the straw on its wool round a steel tumbler. The straight straw touches the tumbler at only one point, with big gaps at both ends.
setup.caption: 2. Wrap it round the tumbler. Count the pieces that touch.

setup.art: The straw cut into 2, then 4, then 8 pieces, each set threaded on wool, lying in a row on the table.
setup.caption: 3. Cut the straw into more pieces and test again.

setup.art: Eight short straw pieces on wool hugging a steel tumbler almost all the way round, with tiny gaps.
setup.caption: 4. With 8 pieces, the chain hugs the tumbler.

flow.do: 1. Wrap tape round one end of the wool to make a stiff tip. 2. Push the tip through the straw. 3. Tie a big knot at the other end.
flow.say: This straw is our pretend backbone. The wool is like the spinal cord that runs through the middle of your own backbone.
flow.kid: Push the wool through the straw. This is your pretend backbone.

flow.do: Show the four chains you will test: 1, 2, 4 and 8 pieces. Ask for a guess and a reason. Write the guess down.
flow.say: We will cut the straw into more and more pieces. Which one will wrap round the tumbler best? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess. Which will wrap round the tumbler best? Why?

good: Eight pieces, because it can bend in more places.
One piece, because it is strong.

flow.parent: Any guess is fine, as long as there is a reason. Do not tell your child what will happen.

flow.do: 1. Hold the tumbler still. 2. Wrap the straw round it. 3. Pull both ends of the wool gently. 4. Count the pieces that touch the tumbler. 5. Try to fit fingers in the biggest gap.
flow.say: Wrap it round the tumbler and pull the wool gently. How many pieces touch the tumbler? How many fingers fit in the gap?
flow.kid: Wrap it round the tumbler. Count the pieces that touch. Fit your fingers in the gap.
flow.parent: A whole straw stays nearly straight. It touches the tumbler at one point, and three or four fingers fit in the gap at each end. A thin plastic straw may kink if you pull hard. A kink is a fold, not a joint, so pull gently, or use the rolled newspaper tube.

flow.do: 1. Pull the straw off the wool. 2. Cut it in half. 3. Thread both pieces and test again. 4. Cut each piece in half again for 4 pieces, then again for 8. Test each time.
flow.say: Now cut it in half and test again. Then cut again. What changes each time?
flow.kid: Cut the straw in half. Test again. Then cut again and test.

ask.q: What happens as you add more pieces?
good: It bends round more.
The gaps get smaller.
More pieces touch the tumbler.

flow.parent: Usually 2 pieces make a bent V and touch at 2 places. 4 pieces make a square-ish shape. 8 short pieces hug the tumbler almost all the way round, with gaps too small for a finger. Each joint only tilts a little, but more joints add up to a bigger curve. Keep the pull on the wool gentle, so it does not snap. Cutting and threading three times is fiddly, so the grown-up helps with the scissors and the wool.

flow.do: 1. Look at the results table together. 2. Ask what your child thinks, what they saw, and why.
flow.say: Which chain bent best? Was your guess right? Why can a backbone bend?
flow.kid: Which chain bent best? Why?

ask.q: Why can your back bend, if every bone in it is hard?
good: Because it is many small bones, and each one tilts a little.
Like the 8-piece straw, it bends at lots of joints.

flow.parent: A strong answer uses the evidence: 'The 8-piece chain hugged the tumbler, but the whole straw stayed straight. A backbone has many bones, so it bends at many joints.' Now read the card on what a backbone is.

check.q: A snake can curl up into rings. What does the Bendy Backbone test tell you about a snake's backbone?
options: It is one long, soft bone
It has a great many small vertebrae
It has no bones at all
check.why: In your test, more pieces made a rounder curve. A snake has a few hundred vertebrae, so they can coil tightly. If you chose 'no bones', remember that snakes are vertebrates: they have a backbone.

experiments.title: The Clue Test: which clue sorts animals into their groups?
experiments.context: In this experiment you sort 18 animal cards three times, each time by a different clue: where they live, how they move, and what covers their body. A colour dot on the back of each card shows the animal's true group. You count which clue mixes up the groups least.
experiments.question: Which clue sorts animals into their true groups best: where they live, how they move, or what covers their body?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Which clue will put the animals with their own group: where they live, how they move, or what covers their body? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: We use the same 18 cards every time. Only the clue changes. We count the colours on each mat the same way every time. Then we add them up. Five colours in all would mean every group stayed together.

materials.item: 18 small pieces of paper, for cards
crayons or sketch pens in blue, green, brown, red and yellow
5 sheets of old paper or newspaper, for mats
a pencil and paper for the results

schedule.what: Make 18 cards. Sort them by where they live, by how they move, and by body covering. Count the colours on each mat each time.

experiments.record: Fill in the results table. Circle the clue with the fewest colours in all.

setup.art: Eighteen small paper cards on a table, each with an animal name and a quick drawing, and a coloured crayon dot on the back of some cards.
setup.caption: 1. Make 18 animal cards, with a colour dot on the back for the true group.

setup.art: Three sheets of paper on the floor labelled 'Water', 'Land' and 'Air', with animal cards placed on them.
setup.caption: 2. Sort the cards by one clue at a time.

setup.art: Cards on a mat turned over to show their dots: blue, brown, red and yellow dots all mixed together.
setup.caption: 3. Turn the cards over. Count the colours on each mat.

flow.do: 1. Write the 18 names from the list in the grown-up note below, one on each card. 2. Your child adds a tiny picture to each. 3. Out of sight, put a coloured dot on the back of each card.
flow.say: Add a tiny picture to each card. I will put a secret colour on the back. It shows the animal's true group.
flow.kid: Add a tiny picture to each card. Do not look at the backs!
flow.parent: The 18 animals: sardine, shark, seahorse, frog, toad, tree frog, house gecko, cobra, crocodile, sea turtle, crow, duck, peacock, bat, river dolphin, cow, pangolin, you. Dots: blue for sardine, shark, seahorse. Green for frog, toad, tree frog. Brown for gecko, cobra, crocodile, turtle. Red for crow, duck, peacock. Yellow for bat, river dolphin, cow, pangolin, you.

flow.do: Ask for a guess and a reason. Write it down.
flow.say: We will sort by three clues. Which clue will keep each group together best? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess. Which clue will keep the groups together? Why?

good: Where they live, because fish all live in water.
The covering, because fish have scales and birds have feathers.

flow.do: 1. Lay 3 mats: Water, Land, Air. 2. Your child puts each card where that animal spends most time. 3. Turn the cards over and count the colours on each mat. 4. Add them up.
flow.say: First clue: where do they live? Put each animal on Water, Land or Air. Now turn them over. How many colours on each mat?
flow.kid: Sort by where they live. Turn the cards over. Count the colours.
flow.parent: There is no wrong place if your child has a reason. Usually the Water mat gets 4 or 5 colours, because the dolphin, turtle, crocodile and duck join the fish. The total is usually about 10 or 11.

flow.do: 1. Lay 3 mats: Swims, Walks or crawls, Flies. 2. Sort again. 3. Turn over, count and add up.
flow.say: Second clue: how do they move? Does this clue mix the groups more, or less?
flow.kid: Sort by how they move. Count the colours again.
flow.parent: The bat goes with the birds, and the dolphin and turtle swim with the fish. The total is usually about 9 or 10.

flow.do: 1. Lay 5 mats: Fins and wet scales, Smooth damp skin, Dry scales or a shell, Feathers, Hair or fur. 2. Sort again. 3. Turn over, count and add up.
flow.say: Third clue: what covers the body? Look at each mat. Which animals are still mixed up?
flow.kid: Sort by what covers the body. Count the colours again.

ask.q: Which animals are still in the wrong place?
good: The pangolin is with the reptiles.
The dolphin is with the frogs.

flow.parent: Usually only two cards are mixed up. The pangolin goes on dry scales, and the dolphin on smooth skin. The total is usually about 7.

flow.do: 1. Add one more clue: does the mother feed the babies milk? 2. Move every milk animal to the Hair or fur mat. 3. Count again. 4. Ask what your child thinks, what they saw, and why.
flow.say: Now add one more clue. Which animals drink milk as babies? Move them. How many colours now? What did you find?
flow.kid: Move the milk animals to Hair or fur. Count again. What did you find?
flow.parent: Now there should be 5 colours in all, one on each mat. A strong answer says: 'Where they live gave 11 colours in all. Covering gave 7. Covering and milk together got all 5 groups right.'

check.q: In the Clue Test, a pangolin went on the Dry scales mat with the reptiles. Which clue moved her to the mammals?
check.why: Only mammal mothers make milk. Lizards also live on land and have four legs, so those clues cannot tell a pangolin from a lizard.

activities.title: Find Your Own Backbone
activities.context: In this short activity you find your own backbone with your fingers. You feel the bumps of your vertebrae in your neck and down your back.

materials.item: a grown-up or an older child to help

schedule.what: Feel the bumps on the back of your neck, then down a grown-up's back while they bend forward.

activities.record: Draw a person from behind, with a row of dots for the backbone.

setup.art: A girl touching the back of her own neck while she nods her head forward.
setup.caption: 1. Nod your head and feel the back of your neck.

setup.art: A boy bending forward to touch his toes while a friend runs her fingers down the bumps on his back.
setup.caption: 2. Feel the bumps down a bent back.

flow.do: Your child puts their fingers on the back of their neck and nods their head forward slowly.
flow.say: Put your fingers on the back of your neck. Now nod your head down slowly. What do you feel?
flow.kid: Touch the back of your neck. Nod your head down. Feel the bump?
flow.parent: Most people can feel one big bump at the bottom of the neck when they nod. That is a vertebra.

flow.do: A grown-up or older child bends forward. Your child runs a finger down the middle of their back and counts the bumps they can feel.
flow.say: Now feel my back as I bend. Count the bumps you can feel. Are they joined, or separate?
flow.kid: Feel the grown-up's back as they bend. Count the bumps.

ask.q: How many bumps did you count?
good: About 10 or 15.
Too many to count.

flow.parent: Most children feel 10 to 20 bumps. The backbone has 33 vertebrae in all, but some are hard to feel. The bumps stand out more when the back bends, because the bones tilt apart a little.

activities.title: Seven Neck Bones: a paper chain giraffe and you
activities.context: In this activity you make two paper chains for two necks: yours and a giraffe's. Both chains have 7 rings, because a giraffe and you both have 7 neck bones.

materials.item: strips of old newspaper or paper, some short and some long
glue or sticky tape
a crayon to draw a head

schedule.what: Make a 7-ring chain from short strips and a 7-ring chain from long strips. Compare them.

activities.record: The two paper chains, with a drawing of a head on top of each.

setup.art: Fourteen paper strips on a table: seven short ones as long as a finger and seven long ones as long as a forearm.
setup.caption: 1. Cut 7 short strips and 7 long strips.

setup.art: Two paper chains hanging side by side, a short one with a child's head drawn on top and a tall one with a giraffe's head on top, each with 7 rings.
setup.caption: 2. Make two chains of 7 rings. Add a head to each.

flow.do: Ask your child to guess who has more neck bones: a giraffe or a person.
flow.say: A giraffe has a very long neck. Do you think a giraffe has more neck bones than you, or the same?
flow.kid: Guess. Does a giraffe have more neck bones than you?

flow.do: 1. Cut 7 short strips, each as long as your child's finger. 2. Cut 7 long strips, each as long as their forearm. 3. Make each set into a chain of rings. 4. Draw a head for each chain.
flow.say: Make a short chain for your neck and a long chain for a giraffe's neck. Count the rings in each.
flow.kid: Make two chains. Count 7 rings in each.
flow.parent: Nearly every mammal has 7 neck bones, from a mouse to a giraffe. A giraffe's neck bones are each longer than your hand.

flow.do: Hang the chains side by side and talk about them.
flow.say: Both chains have 7 rings. So how is the giraffe's neck so long?
flow.kid: Both have 7. Why is the giraffe's neck so long?

ask.q: Why is the giraffe's neck longer?
good: Each bone is much longer.
The rings are bigger, not more.

activities.title: A Real Fish Backbone (if your family eats fish)
activities.context: If your family cooks fish, this activity lets you see a real backbone. A grown-up lifts the backbone out of a cooked fish. You look at the small bones and bend the backbone gently.

materials.item: a cooked fish with the bones still in, such as a mackerel, a sardine or a pomfret
a steel plate

activities.safety: Fish bones are thin and sharp. A grown-up lifts the bone out. Wash hands after touching it.

schedule.what: After a fish meal, lift out the backbone. Count the small bones and bend the backbone gently.

activities.record: A drawing of the fish backbone, with the small bones in a row.

setup.art: A grown-up's hands lifting a whole backbone out of a cooked mackerel on a steel plate.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up lifts out the backbone.

setup.art: A fish backbone on a steel plate, bending gently into a curve between two fingers.
setup.caption: 2. Look closely, then bend it gently.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up holds the tail of the cooked fish and lifts the backbone out in one piece. 2. Put the backbone on a clean plate.
flow.say: This is the fish's backbone. Look closely. Is it one long bone?
flow.kid: Look at the fish's backbone. Is it one long bone?

flow.do: Your child counts the small bones in the row and bends the backbone gently.
flow.say: Count the small bones in the row. Then hold both ends and bend it very gently. What happens?
flow.kid: Count the small bones. Bend it gently. What happens?

ask.q: Why can the fish's backbone bend?
good: It is made of many small bones.
Each little bone moves a bit.

flow.parent: Most fish have a few dozen vertebrae. A child may lose count, and that is fine. The thin bones sticking out are ribs and spines that held the fish's muscles and fins.

activities.title: My Hand of Five: a five-finger chart
activities.context: In this activity you draw round your hand. Each finger becomes one of the five groups of vertebrates. You write one clue and draw one animal for each.

materials.item: a sheet of paper
a pencil and crayons

schedule.what: Draw round your hand. Label each finger with a group, a clue and an animal.

activities.record: The hand chart, with five groups, five clues and five animals.

setup.art: A child drawing round her hand with a pencil on a sheet of paper.
setup.caption: 1. Draw round your hand.

setup.art: A hand outline with a small drawing on each finger: a fish, a frog, a lizard, a bird and a child, with one word under each.
setup.caption: 2. Give each finger a group, a clue and an animal.

flow.do: Your child draws round one hand.
flow.say: Draw round your hand. You have five fingers, and there are five groups of animals with a backbone.
flow.kid: Draw round your hand. Five fingers, five groups!

flow.do: For each finger, help your child write the group, one clue and draw one animal. Thumb: fish, gills. Pointing finger: amphibians, damp skin. Middle finger: reptiles, dry scales. Ring finger: birds, feathers. Little finger: mammals, milk.
flow.say: Which group goes on your thumb? What clue helps you know a fish? Draw one.
flow.kid: Write a group on each finger. Add a clue. Draw an animal.

good: The mammal finger, because I have hair and drank milk.

flow.parent: Let your child choose the animals. Help with the writing if needed. Keep the hand chart on the wall to look at.

rules: Draw the animal quickly on the front of each card, under its name.
Mix the cards and put them face down in a pile.
One player is the keeper. The keeper takes the top card and reads the back secretly. The back has the clues.
The others take turns to ask one question each about the animal's body. The keeper may answer only yes or no, using the clues on the back.
Good questions are about clues: Does the animal have feathers? Does the mother make milk? Does the animal have gills?
When someone thinks they know the group, they say it. Then they try to guess the animal.
The player who guesses the animal wins the card and is the next keeper. A wrong guess means that player cannot guess again for this card.
If nobody has guessed after 15 questions, or everyone has guessed wrongly, the keeper keeps the card. The next keeper is the player on the keeper's left. With two players, you simply swap.
When the pile is finished, the player with the most cards wins.

setup.art: Twenty small cards on a table, each with an animal name and a quick drawing, being cut out with children's scissors.
setup.caption: 1. Cut out the cards and draw each animal.

setup.art: A girl holding a card close to her chest while two other players ask questions, with a pile of cards on the table.
setup.caption: 2. The keeper hides a card. The others ask yes-or-no questions.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the 20 cards. 2. Share them and draw a quick animal on each.
flow.say: Let's draw the animals first. You draw some, and I will draw some.
flow.kid: Draw an animal on each card.

flow.do: Play one round with the grown-up as the keeper, to show how it works.
flow.say: I have a secret animal. Ask me yes-or-no questions. Try to find the group first.
flow.kid: Ask yes-or-no questions. Find the group first!

ask.q: What is a good first question?
good: Does the animal have feathers?
Does the mother make milk?

flow.parent: Questions about clues work better than guesses. 'Does the animal have feathers?' cuts the animals in two. 'Is the animal a crow?' rules out only one animal.

flow.do: Take turns being the keeper. Try to find the animal in as few questions as you can.
flow.say: Your turn to be the keeper. How few questions can we do it in?
flow.kid: Now you are the keeper. Answer only yes or no.
flow.parent: The pangolin, bat and river dolphin are the tricky cards. If someone asks 'Does the animal have scales?' about the pangolin, the answer is yes. Then the milk question shows she is a mammal.

check.q: Which question tells you fastest if an animal is a bird?
options: Does the animal have two eyes?
check.why: Only birds have feathers. Bats fly too, and almost every animal has two eyes, so those questions do not tell you.

games.title: Odd One Out: four animals, one does not fit
games.context: This is a quick thinking game. Each card shows four animals. Three are in the same group, and one is not. Players find the odd one out and say which clue gave it away.

printables.title: 12 odd-one-out cards to cut out, with the answer on the back

items.b: Bat. A bat is a mammal with fur. The others are birds.
River dolphin. She is a mammal who breathes air. The others are fish.

items.f: Frog, toad, house gecko, tree frog
items.b: House gecko. A gecko is a reptile with dry scales. The others are amphibians.
Frog. A frog is an amphibian with damp skin. The others are reptiles.
Cobra. A cobra is a reptile. The others are mammals.
Butterfly. A butterfly has wings but no backbone. The others are birds.
Sardine. A sardine has a backbone. The others are invertebrates.
Crocodile. A crocodile is a reptile. The others are mammals, humans too.
Turtle. A turtle is a reptile who breathes air. The others are fish.
Duck. A duck is a bird. The others are mammals.
Peacock. A peacock is a bird. The others are reptiles.
Toad. A toad has a backbone. The others are invertebrates.

rules: Put the cards face up in a pile, so the four animals show.
One player reads the four animals aloud.
Everyone thinks quietly. Then everyone points at the odd one out at the same time.
Each player who points at the right animal and says one clue gets a point.
Turn the card over and read the answer aloud to check.
The player with the most points after all 12 cards wins.

setup.art: A card showing four small drawings in a row: a crow, a sparrow, a bat and a peacock.
setup.caption: 1. Read the four animals aloud.

setup.art: Three players all pointing at the bat on the card at the same moment.
setup.caption: 2. Everyone points at the odd one out, then says a clue.

flow.do: Cut out the 12 cards. Read out the first card.
flow.say: Crow, sparrow, bat, peacock. Three are in the same group. Which one is not?
flow.kid: Listen to the four animals. Which one does not fit?

flow.do: Play through the cards. After each, ask which clue gave the answer away.
flow.say: Point together: one, two, three! Now tell me a clue. How do you know?
flow.kid: Point at the odd one out. Say a clue.

ask.q: Why is the bat the odd one out?
good: The bat has fur, and the others have feathers.
The bat is a mammal.

flow.parent: The best answers name a clue, like 'fur, not feathers', not just the group. The cards with no-backbone animals, like the butterfly and the crab, remind your child about invertebrates.

check.q: Frog, toad, house gecko, tree frog. Which is the odd one out?
check.why: A house gecko has dry scales, so the gecko is a reptile. Frogs, toads and tree frogs have smooth, damp skin, so they are amphibians.

projects.title: Five Dough Animals on One Backbone
projects.context: In this two-day project you make five dough animals, one from each group: a fish, a frog, a lizard, a bird and a person. Each animal is built round a backbone of straw pieces. Then you give each one the right covering.

materials.item: a ball of atta dough, about two fists' worth
drinking straws, cut into short pieces, or uncooked macaroni
wool or thread
a pen cap, for pressing scales
a few scraps of paper, for feathers
a few strands of wool, for hair

schedule.what: Make five backbones of threaded straw pieces. Wrap dough round each to make a fish, a frog, a lizard, a bird and a person.
Add the coverings: pressed scales, smooth skin, paper feathers and wool hair. Make a label for each group and show someone at home.

projects.record: A row of five dough animals with labels, and a photo or drawing of them.

setup.art: Five short chains of straw pieces on wool lying on a table, next to a ball of atta dough.
setup.caption: 1. Make five backbones from straw pieces.

setup.art: Five dough animals in a row: a fish with pressed scales, a smooth frog, a scaly lizard, a bird with paper feathers and a person with wool hair, each with a paper label.
setup.caption: 2. Add a covering and a label to each.

flow.do: 1. Thread 5 short chains of straw pieces. 2. Make the fish chain bendy and long. Make the frog chain very short. 3. Wrap dough round each chain to shape the five animals.
flow.say: Every animal here has a backbone. Shall we make the frog's short and the lizard's long?
flow.kid: Make five backbones. Wrap dough round each one.
flow.parent: A frog's backbone is very short, with about nine vertebrae. A lizard's goes on into a long tail. Let your child shape the bodies freely.

flow.do: 1. Press scales on the fish and lizard with a pen cap. 2. Wet the frog with a damp finger. 3. Stick paper feathers on the bird and wool hair on the person. 4. Write a label for each.
flow.say: Now give each animal the right covering. Which one gets feathers? Which one stays smooth and damp?
flow.kid: Give each animal the right covering. Then label them.

ask.q: Which covering does the lizard get, and why?
good: Dry scales, because lizards are reptiles.

flow.wait: Cover the five animals with a damp cloth overnight, so the dough stays soft for pressing scales.

challenges.title: A Backbone That Bends and Stands Up
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. In the Bendy Backbone test, the chain of 8 straw pieces bent round the tumbler. But on loose wool, it flops over and cannot hold up a head. Your back can do both. Can you make a backbone that bends and also stands up?
challenges.problem: Can you make a straw backbone that wraps round a tumbler, and also stands up straight holding a one-rupee coin on top for 10 seconds?
constraints: Use the 8 straw pieces from the test, or pieces like them.
You may use wool, rubber bands, paper, tape and small pieces of eraser or cotton.
The backbone must still bend round the tumbler afterwards.
materials: small pieces of eraser, cardboard or cotton
general: Pull the wool tight and tie it, so the pieces press together. Real backbones are held tight by muscles and strong bands called ligaments.
Stand the chain on a flat base, like a bottle cap or a lump of dough.
creative: Put a small soft pad, like a bit of eraser or folded paper, between the pieces. Your backbone has soft pads called discs between the vertebrae.
Stretch two rubber bands along the sides, like the muscles on each side of your backbone.
challenges.your_turn: Make your own backbone. Test it twice: does it bend round the tumbler, and does it stand up with the coin on top for 10 seconds? Change one thing and test again.

setup.art: A chain of straw pieces on tight wool standing upright on a lump of dough, with a one-rupee coin balanced on top.
setup.caption: 1. Make your backbone stand up with a coin on top.

setup.art: The same chain wrapped round a steel tumbler.
setup.caption: 2. Then check it still bends round the tumbler.

flow.do: Stand the loose 8-piece chain from the test up on the table and let go. Watch it flop.
flow.say: Our chain bent beautifully, but look. It cannot stand up. Your back can bend and stand. How?
flow.kid: Your chain flops. Can you make it bend and stand up?

flow.do: Your child tries their own ideas with the materials.
flow.say: Try one idea. Does it stand with the coin? Does it still bend?
flow.kid: Try an idea. Test it. Change one thing and test again.
flow.parent: Pulling the wool tight is usually the first thing that works. Too tight, and the chain stops bending. Let your child find the balance. It is hard to get both. A chain that stands but bends only a little, or bends well but needs a hand to stand, is still a good result. Your real backbone solves this with discs, ligaments and muscles all working together.

flow.do: Test the best design twice: standing with the coin for 10 seconds, then wrapping round the tumbler.
flow.say: Let's test it both ways. What made it work?
flow.kid: Test it both ways. What made it work?

ask.q: What made your backbone stand and still bend?
good: Pulling the wool tight held the pieces together.
The rubber bands worked like muscles.

items.p: Draw a line from each animal to their group.
items.why: A crow has feathers, a frog has damp skin, a sardine has gills and fins, a cow feeds her calf milk, and a gecko has dry scales.
items.art: Five animals on the left and the five group names on the right, mixed up.

items.p: Sort the animals: backbone, or no backbone?
items.why: Dogs, crows and frogs are vertebrates. Ants, prawns and earthworms are invertebrates. A prawn's hard part is a shell on the outside, not bones inside.
items.art: Six small drawings: a dog, an ant, a crow, a prawn, a frog and an earthworm.

items.p: Remember the Bendy Backbone test. Draw the whole straw and the 8-piece chain wrapped round the tumbler.
items.a: A straight straw touching the tumbler at one point, and a chain of 8 pieces curving close round the tumbler.
items.why: A strong drawing shows big gaps beside the straight straw, and small gaps between the 8-piece chain and the tumbler.
items.art: Two empty circles to draw round, labelled 1 piece and 8 pieces.

items.p: Say out loud, and a grown-up writes it down: why did the 8-piece chain wrap round the tumbler better than the whole straw?
items.a: Because it could bend at many joints. Each piece tilted a little, and the tilts added up.
items.why: A strong answer says the chain bent at the joints between the pieces, and that more joints made a rounder curve.

items.p: Which clue tells you for sure that an animal is a bird?
items.why: Only birds have feathers. Monkeys and squirrels live in trees too, and birds have two legs, not four.

items.p: A snake's skin is slimy and wet.
items.why: False. Snake skin is dry. Snakes are reptiles, with dry scales. Frogs and toads are the ones with damp skin.

items.p: Label the drawing of a child's back: neck, backbone, one vertebra, hips.
a: neck: at the top, under the head
backbone: the row of bones down the middle
one vertebra: one small bone in the row
hips: at the bottom of the backbone
items.why: The backbone runs from the neck to the hips. Each small bone in it is a vertebra.
items.art: A child seen from behind with the backbone drawn as a row of small bones, and four empty label lines.

items.p: Animals with a backbone are called ________.
items.why: Vertebrates are animals with a backbone. Animals without one are invertebrates.

items.p: Lakshmi sells fish at the market in Kochi. Dr Asha is a scientist who studies animals. They sort sea animals in different ways.

views.says: I put fish, prawns and crabs in one basket, because they all come from the sea and people cook them in the same curry.
I sort fish apart from prawns and crabs. Fish have a backbone and gills. Prawns and crabs have no backbone.

items.ask: Which way would you use to sort a market, and which for a science book? Why? Then say one thing the other person has right.
items.a: A strong answer sees that both ways are useful for different jobs. Lakshmi's way helps shoppers and cooks. Dr Asha's way shows which animals have the same kind of body and are related.
items.why: There is more than one good way to sort. The scientist's five groups are best for finding relatives. The seller's way is best for cooking and selling.

items.p: Count the legs: a crow, a cow and a cobra. How many legs in all?
items.why: A crow has 2 legs, a cow has 4 and a cobra has none. 2 and 4 and 0 make 6. Legs alone do not tell you the group.

items.p: A tadpole lives in a pond. What does a tadpole breathe with?
items.why: A tadpole breathes with gills, like a fish. When the tadpole becomes a frog, the frog breathes with lungs and through the damp skin.

items.p: An olive ridley turtle swims in the sea all her life. Why is she not a fish? Give two clues. A grown-up can write down what you say.
items.a: She breathes air with lungs, not gills. She has dry scales and a shell. She lays her eggs on a beach.
items.why: A strong answer gives two clues that show she is a reptile: lungs, dry scales, eggs laid on land.

items.p: Sort by skin: dry scales, or smooth damp skin?
items.why: Geckos, cobras and crocodiles are reptiles, with dry scales. Toads, frogs and tree frogs are amphibians, with skin that has no scales. A toad's skin is bumpy, but still has no scales.
items.art: Six small drawings: a gecko, a toad, a cobra, a frog, a crocodile and a tree frog.

items.p: Put a frog's life in order.
items: A young frog with a short tail
Eggs in jelly in the water
A tadpole with a tail and gills
a: Eggs in jelly in the water
A tadpole with a tail and gills
A tadpole with back legs
A young frog with a short tail
A grown frog
items.why: Eggs, then a tadpole, then legs grow, then the tail shrinks, then a grown frog. Amphibians begin life in water.

items.p: Make up a new reptile and draw them. Show two clues that tell people your animal is a reptile.
items.a: A made-up animal with dry scales, and eggs with shells laid on land, or lungs.
items.why: A strong drawing shows reptile clues, like dry scales and shelled eggs, and leaves out feathers, fur and gills.

items.p: After the Clue Test, Ammu and her friend Divya, both aged 7, argue about the best clue.

views.says: The body covering is the best clue. It put almost every animal in the right group.
Milk is the best clue. It put the pangolin and the dolphin with the mammals.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Use what you found in the Clue Test. Then say one thing the other person has right. A grown-up can write down what you say.
items.a: A strong answer uses the test results. Covering sorted most animals well, so Ammu is partly right. But milk only tells you about mammals, and does nothing for a frog or a lizard. Using both clues together got every animal right.
items.why: Each clue does part of the job. Checking more than one clue works best.

items.p: Label the fish: gills, fin, scales, tail.
a: gills: under the flap behind the eye
fin: on the back and belly
scales: covering the body
tail: at the back end
items.why: Gills take in oxygen from water. Fins steer, the tail pushes, and scales cover and protect the body.
items.art: A drawing of a sardine from the side, with four empty label lines.

items.p: All birds can fly.
items.why: False. Every bird has feathers, but not every bird flies. An ostrich cannot fly, and a hen only flutters a little way.

items.p: Baby frogs and toads are called ________.
items.why: Frogs and toads start life as tadpoles in water, with tails and gills.

items.p: In the Clue Test, when you sorted by where animals live, the mats had 5, 4 and 2 colours. How many colours was that in all?
items.why: 5 and 4 make 9. 9 and 2 make 11. With only 5 groups, 11 colours means the groups were very mixed up.

items.p: A pangolin is covered in scales, like a lizard. Which clues show that she is a mammal? A grown-up can write down what you say.
items.a: She has some hair on her face and belly, and the mother feeds her baby milk.
items.why: A strong answer names milk, and hair if known. Scales alone do not decide the group, because fish, reptiles and pangolins all have them.

items.p: Two scientists argue about where birds belong.

views.says: Birds are a group of their own. Only birds have feathers, and birds make their own body heat.
Birds belong with the reptiles. Birds came from dinosaurs, and a crocodile's closest relatives are birds.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Why? Then say one thing the other scientist has right. A grown-up can write down what you say.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side with a reason, and sees that both are right about something. Feathers make birds easy to tell apart. But birds and crocodiles really are close relatives.
items.why: Scientists really do argue about this. It depends whether groups are for telling animals apart, or for showing who is related to whom.

items.p: A caecilian lives in wet soil in the Western Ghats. They have no legs, smooth damp skin and no scales. Which group are they in?
items.why: Smooth, damp skin with no scales is the amphibian clue. A caecilian has a backbone, so is not an invertebrate. No legs is not enough to make an animal a snake.

items.p: In the Bendy Backbone test you tried 1, 2, 4 and 8 pieces. Predict and draw what a chain of 16 pieces would look like round the tumbler.
items.a: An almost perfect circle round the tumbler, with almost no gaps.
items.why: A strong drawing shows that 16 pieces curve even more closely than 8, because there are even more joints, each tilting a little.
items.art: An empty circle to draw round.

items.p: A snake has a few hundred vertebrae. You have 33. How do so many vertebrae help a snake? A grown-up can write down what you say.
items.a: With so many joints, a snake can bend into tight curves, coil up and wriggle along the ground without legs.
items.why: A strong answer links many vertebrae to many joints, and many joints to a bigger, rounder bend, as in the Bendy Backbone test.

items.p: Every animal that lives in water is a fish.
items.why: False. A river dolphin is a mammal and a sea turtle is a reptile, and both live in water. Tadpoles are amphibians. Where an animal lives is only one clue.

items.p: Sort the animals: lays eggs, or gives birth to babies?
items.why: Birds, most reptiles and amphibians lay eggs. Cows and bats are mammals, and most mammals give birth to babies.
items.art: Six small drawings: a hen, a cow, a cobra, a crocodile, a bat and a frog.

items.p: Label the bird: beak, feathers, wing, legs.
a: beak: the hard mouth at the front
feathers: covering the body
wing: on each side
legs: two, underneath
items.why: A beak, feathers, two wings and two legs are the bird clues. Feathers belong to birds alone.
items.art: A drawing of a crow from the side, with four empty label lines.

items.p: Put these animals in order, from the fewest vertebrae to the most.
a: a frog
you
a snake
items.why: A frog has about nine vertebrae, you have 33, and a snake has a few hundred.

items.p: Which of these animals is an invertebrate?
items.why: A crab has a hard shell outside and no backbone. A shark is a fish and a toad is an amphibian, so both have a backbone.

quiz.p: What is your backbone made of?
opts: A chain of many small bones
quiz.why: Your backbone is a chain of 33 small bones called vertebrae. You can feel them as bumps when you bend.

quiz.p: In the Bendy Backbone test, which chain wrapped round the tumbler best?
quiz.why: More pieces meant more joints. Each joint tilted a little, and together they curved round the tumbler.

quiz.p: Which of these is a vertebrate?
quiz.why: A crow has a backbone, so is a vertebrate. Ants and prawns have no backbone.

quiz.p: Which group has smooth, damp skin and starts life as tadpoles?
quiz.why: Frogs and toads are amphibians. They have smooth, damp skin and begin life in water as tadpoles.

quiz.p: How does a fish take in oxygen?
quiz.why: A fish takes water in through the mouth and over the gills. The gills take oxygen from the water.

quiz.p: What is true of every mammal?
opts: The mothers feed their babies milk
They lay eggs with hard shells
quiz.why: Every mammal mother makes milk for her young. Only a few mammals fly, and birds are the ones that lay hard-shelled eggs.

quiz.p: A bat flies with wings. Which group is a bat in?
opts: Mammals, because bats have fur and drink milk
Reptiles, because bats like the dark
quiz.why: Flying is only one clue. A bat has fur, and the mother feeds her baby milk, so a bat is a mammal.

quiz.p: A house gecko lives near the tube light. What covers a gecko's skin?
quiz.why: A gecko is a reptile, with skin covered in tiny dry scales.

opts: We are not in any animal group
quiz.why: Humans have hair, breathe air and drink milk as babies. So we are mammals, and mammals are animals.

quiz.p: In the Clue Test, which clue mixed up the groups the most?
quiz.why: Sorting by where they live put the dolphin, turtle, crocodile and duck with the fish. Body covering kept most groups together.

quiz.p: A river dolphin is a fish because she lives in water.
quiz.why: False. A river dolphin breathes air and her baby drinks her milk. She is a mammal, even though she lives in water.

quiz.p: How many bones are in a giraffe's neck?
quiz.why: A giraffe has 7 neck bones, the same number as you. Each of the giraffe's bones is just much longer.

applications: Doctors and physiotherapists check how a person's backbone bends, to help people with back pain move well again.
Engineers have built snake robots with many small joints in a row, like a backbone, to crawl into pipes and broken buildings.
Wildlife rescuers must know an animal's group to care for them. A turtle needs air and a dry place to lay eggs, but a fish needs water over the gills.
Scientists count frogs and toads to check that ponds and streams are clean, because amphibians take in water through their damp skin.
Fish sellers and cooks cut along the backbone to clean a fish, because the backbone runs down the middle of the body.

open_questions.q: Why did the first animals grow a backbone?
open_questions.why_open: The first animals with a backbone lived in the sea more than 500 million years ago. Scientists think a backbone may have helped them swim, or protected the nerve cord, but the fossils do not tell us for sure.

open_questions.q: How many kinds of frogs live in India?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists keep finding new ones. In 2017 the Indian scientist Sonali Garg and her team named seven new night frogs from the Western Ghats. Some are tiny frogs. Many more may still be waiting to be found.

open_questions.q: What is it like to be a fish?
open_questions.why_open: Fish feel pain and fear, and they learn and remember. But fish sense the world through water, with gills, a sense of touch along the side of the body and eyes made for water. What that feels like from the inside, nobody knows.

maths.problem: In the Bendy Backbone test, 1 piece touched the tumbler at 1 place, and 2 pieces at 2 places. 4 pieces touched at 4 places. How many places for 8 pieces?
maths.explain: Each piece touched the tumbler once. So the number of places is the same as the number of pieces: 1, 2, 4, 8. Each time we cut every piece in half, the number doubles.
maths.context: This is about the Bendy Backbone test, where you cut a straw into more and more pieces and wrapped it round a tumbler.
maths.why_maths: Spotting the pattern lets you predict what more pieces would do without cutting them.

maths.problem: In the Clue Test, sorting by where animals live gave 11 colours in all. Sorting by body covering gave 7. Which clue mixed up the groups less, and by how many colours?
maths.explain: Count on from 7 to 11: 8, 9, 10, 11. That is 4. Fewer colours means fewer groups mixed up, so body covering was the better clue.
maths.context: This is about the Clue Test, where you sorted 18 animal cards by different clues and counted the colours on each mat.
maths.why_maths: Finding the difference shows how much better one clue was, not just which one won.

maths.problem: Draw two overlapping circles. One is 'Lives in water'. The other is 'Has a backbone'. Where do these go: a sardine, a prawn, a crow, a frog, a crab?
maths.answer: Sardine and frog in the middle, where the circles overlap. Prawn and crab in 'Lives in water' only. Crow in 'Has a backbone' only.
maths.explain: A sardine lives in water and has a backbone. A frog lives in and near water and has a backbone. Prawns and crabs live in water but have no backbone. A crow has a backbone but does not live in water.
maths.context: This is about sorting animals by two clues at once, as in the Clue Test.
maths.why_maths: Overlapping circles show that one animal can belong to two groups at once, which is why one clue alone can fool you.

maths.problem: In the story, Meenakshi, her little brother Kiran, her mother Amma and her grandmother Ajji each have 7 bones in the neck. How many neck bones do these four people have in all?
maths.explain: There are 4 people with 7 each. 7 and 7 make 14. 14 and 14 make 28.
maths.context: This is about the story of Meenakshi's family, and the paper chain activity, where you found that people and giraffes all have 7 neck bones.
maths.why_maths: Adding equal groups is a quick way to count the same thing in many bodies.

science: Human vertebral column: 33 vertebrae (7 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 fused sacral, about 4 fused coccygeal), with intervertebral discs and the spinal cord running through the vertebral canal.

Seven cervical vertebrae in almost all mammals, including giraffes; exceptions are some sloths and manatees. F. Galis, 'Why do almost all mammals have seven cervical vertebrae?', Journal of Experimental Zoology 285 (1999).
Snakes have from about 100 to over 400 vertebrae. Frogs (Anura) have a short column of usually 5 to 9 presacral vertebrae, a sacral vertebra and a urostyle.
Vertebrates are about 5% of described animal species, and fish are about half of all vertebrate species.

Linnaeus, Systema Naturae, 10th edition (1758), class Amphibia including frogs, lizards, snakes, turtles and crocodiles. A. Brongniart, 'Essai d'une classification naturelle des reptiles' (1800), separating the Batrachia (frogs and toads) from the other reptiles by their naked skin and metamorphosis.

Fish pain: L. U. Sneddon, V. A. Braithwaite and M. J. Gentle, 'Do fishes have nociceptors? Evidence for the evolution of a vertebrate sensory system', Proceedings of the Royal Society B 270 (2003). Opposing view: B. Key, 'Why fish do not feel pain', Animal Sentience (2016).
New night frogs: S. Garg and others, 'Seven new species of Night Frogs (Anura, Nyctibatrachidae) from the Western Ghats Biodiversity Hotspot of India', PeerJ (2017).
Purple frog Nasikabatrachus sahyadrensis, described by S. D. Biju and F. Bossuyt in Nature (2003). Caecilians (Gymnophiona) in the Western Ghats and Northeast India.

Indian pangolin (Manis crassicaudata): keratin scales with hair on the face and underside, young carried on the mother's tail or back. Ganga river dolphin (Platanista gangetica) declared India's national aquatic animal in 2009. Russell's viper gives birth to live young. Olive ridley mass nesting at Rushikulya and Gahirmatha, Odisha. Draco dussumieri, the gliding lizard of the Western Ghats.
Samyutta Nikaya 5.10 (Vajira Sutta). Tirukkural 322. Nyaya-Vaisheshika view of the whole (avayavin) as distinct from its parts, against Buddhist views.

roots.context: We have learnt that a backbone is a chain of small bones, and that every fish, amphibian, reptile, bird and mammal has one. Now we ask what the Bendy Backbone test tells us about bodies, and about ourselves.

deep_truth.truth: You felt many separate bumps down your back. Your straw backbone hugged the tumbler only when cut into many short pieces. Each piece tilts a little, and together the tilts make a big curve. A backbone bends because it is a chain of many hard bones.
deep_truth.habit: We say 'backbone', one word, as if it were one stiff bone. In fact it is a chain of many small vertebrae, and the bending happens at the joints between them.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Bendy Backbone test, the whole straw stayed straight and touched the tumbler at one point, while 8 pieces wrapped round it. When a grown-up bends forward, the bumps of the vertebrae spread apart and stand out. A cooked fish's backbone lifts out as a row of tiny bones that can bend.

three.who_am_i: You are a mammal, an animal with a backbone of 33 small bones. When you bend, they all tilt together.
three.what_is_life: Every fish, frog, lizard, bird and mammal is built round the same kind of chain of bones.
three.what_is_this_world: The world is full of backbones of every length: a frog's short one, a snake's long one and yours.

roots.thread: More than 500 million years ago, the first animals with a backbone swam in the sea. Every fish, frog, lizard, bird and mammal alive today comes from them, humans too. The same plan, a chain of small bones, has grown into a snake's coil, a frog's short, stiff back, a giraffe's tall neck and your own bending spine.

teachings.teaching: Vajira, a Buddhist nun, taught that the word 'chariot' is a name we give to many parts put together. In the same way, she said, 'a being' is a name for many parts.
teachings.link: In this unit, 'backbone' is one word for a chain of many vertebrae. The bending you felt happens at the joints between the parts.

teachings.teaching: Thiruvalluvar, the Tamil poet, wrote that sharing your food and caring for the many kinds of living beings is the greatest of all teachings.
teachings.link: Fish, frogs, lizards, birds and mammals are the many kinds of beings with a backbone, and humans are one of them. Knowing how each group lives, wet skin or dry, water or air, is a first step in caring for them.

science.text: All animals with a backbone come from the same ancestors, small fish-like animals who lived in the sea more than 500 million years ago.
Almost every mammal, from a mouse to a giraffe, has 7 neck vertebrae. Why mammals keep to 7, when birds and reptiles have many different numbers, is still argued about.

other_view.who: The Nyaya thinkers of ancient India
other_view.view: The Nyaya school argued about this with Buddhist thinkers. They said a whole, like a cloth, is a real thing of its own, not only its threads. In this view, your backbone really is one thing, made of many bones.

practice.title: Bend Like a Chain
practice.say: Kneel on your hands and knees, like a cat. Breathe in slowly and let your tummy sink down, with your head up. Breathe out slowly and round your back up high, with your head down. Do it three times, very slowly. Feel each part of your back move, one after the other. Now sit up tall and still. Your whole chain of bones is holding you up.
practice.kid: Get on your hands and knees, like a cat. Breathe in. Let your tummy sink. Breathe out. Round your back up high. Do it three times, slowly. Feel each part of your back move. Now sit up tall.

ask: Your backbone is many bones. Is it one thing, or many things?

how_we_found_out.story: About 270 years ago, people did not sort frogs apart from lizards. In 1758, the Swedish scientist Carl Linnaeus wrote a famous book that named and sorted animals. He put frogs, toads, lizards, snakes, turtles and crocodiles together in one group. He called the group Amphibia. Many people agreed, and frogs and lizards stayed in one group for many years. Then, in 1800, a young French scientist called Alexandre Brongniart looked again. He saw that frogs and toads have bare, damp skin with no scales. He saw that their young are tadpoles, who live in water and slowly change their shape to become frogs. Lizards, snakes, turtles and crocodiles have dry, scaly skin, and their young hatch looking like small adults. Brongniart put frogs and toads in a group of their own. Later scientists agreed, and made the frogs' group a whole class, with the name amphibians. The lizards, snakes, turtles and crocodiles became the reptiles. Brongniart looked at more than one clue, and that is how the two groups were told apart.
how_we_found_out.who: Carl Linnaeus, a Swedish scientist, and Alexandre Brongniart, a French scientist
how_we_found_out.when: Linnaeus sorted frogs and reptiles together in 1758. Brongniart split them apart in 1800.
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That frogs, toads, lizards, snakes, turtles and crocodiles all belong in one group. Looking closely at skin and at how the young grow up showed that frogs and toads are a different group.
